document.summary: Cloudflare's CN Turnstile endpoint is real, is genuinely faster from mainland China, and is unusable for almost everyone — because a widget's region is fixed at creation and gated behind China Network. Test sitekeys hide this.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content:
`challenges.cloudflare-cn.com` is a real Cloudflare Turnstile host that routes through Cloudflare's China datacenters, and it is noticeably faster from a mainland China network. It is also unusable with an ordinary sitekey.

The reason is not rate limits, domain allowlists, or account tier as such. Every Turnstile widget carries a **`region`** — `world` or `china` — that is chosen when the widget is created and can never be changed, and each host only serves keys of its own region. Creating a `region: "china"` widget requires an entitlement that comes with a China Network contract.

What makes this worth writing down is the trap: Cloudflare's public *test* sitekeys work on the CN host, so the obvious way to try this out reports success and tells you nothing about whether your real key will work. It will not.

sections.title: How did I find this
sections.content:
I was playing around with [crt.name](https://crt.name), searching for half-public services, when I stumbled on `challenges.cloudflare-cn.com`. It serves the same content as `challenges.cloudflare.com` — including the Turnstile bundle at `/turnstile/v0/api.js` — so it looked like a straightforward mirror of the global host.

Both hosts 302 the script to the *same* build (`/turnstile/v0/b/<hash>/api.js`), which reinforced that impression. The bundle is byte-identical. Only the challenge traffic differs, and that is where the whole thing falls apart.

sections.title: Testing the finding
sections.content:
I built a minimal page embedding the widget with a [test sitekey](https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/get-started/client-side-rendering/), then added `-cn` to the host. It worked, and it was visibly faster on a native China network. `cdn-cgi/trace` and the `CF-RAY` suffix confirmed why: requests to the CN host land in [Cloudflare's China datacenters](https://www.cloudflare.com/products/china-network/) (I saw `-XIY`, Xi'an) rather than the nearest global edge.

That result is a false positive. The CN host keeps its own set of recognised sitekeys, and Cloudflare's hardcoded test keys are in it. Testing with a test key proves only that test keys work.

Asking the challenge endpoint directly is more honest. Same path, same headers, only the host and the sitekey vary:

```
GET https://challenges.cloudflare{,-cn}.com/cdn-cgi/challenge-platform
      /h/b/turnstile/f/av0/rch/ch2aa/<SITEKEY>/auto/fbE/new/normal?lang=auto
```

| Sitekey | `cloudflare.com` | `cloudflare-cn.com` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `1x00000000000000000000AA` (test) | 200 | 200 |
| `2x00000000000000000000AB` (test) | 200 | 200 |
| `3x00000000000000000000FF` (test) | 200 | 200 |
| `0x4AAAAAAAAjq6WYeRDKmebM` (Cloudflare's own demo key) | 200 | **400** |
| a real production sitekey | 200 | **400** |
| `0x4AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA` (does not exist) | 400 | 400 |

On the CN host, a real sitekey is indistinguishable from one that does not exist. Cloudflare's *own* demo key fails there too — tested with its own referer — so this is not about one account, one domain allowlist, or one deployment.

In a browser the 400 surfaces as `[Cloudflare Turnstile] Error: 400020`, usually alongside a `postMessage` origin-mismatch warning and a CSP complaint. Both are downstream noise: the CSP error comes from Cloudflare's own 400 page violating the CSP Cloudflare set on it, and the origin mismatch happens because the challenge iframe never became a `cloudflare-cn.com` document at all.

sections.title: Why it fails: the region field
sections.content:
The Turnstile widget API explains it. `POST /accounts/{account_id}/challenges/widgets` accepts:

```json
"region": {
  "description": "Region where this widget can be used. This cannot be changed after creation.",
  "default": "world",
  "enum": ["world", "china"]
}
```

Three consequences, each confirmed against the live API:

1. **A widget only works on the host matching its region.** A `region: "world"` key is what almost everyone has, and the CN host rejects it.
2. **`region` is immutable.** `PUT` accepts the field but the server refuses: `invalid value for 'region': you cannot change region`. An existing global widget can never be promoted — a China widget has to be *created* as one.
3. **Creating one is entitled.** `POST` with `region: "china"` on an ordinary account returns `not entitled to create widgets with this region`. The entitlement comes with a [China Network](https://developers.cloudflare.com/china-network/) contract, which is an Enterprise arrangement involving ICP filing and Cloudflare's in-country partner network.

Cloudflare documents the outcome plainly, in the China Network product's own list of available products — footnote 1: *"Turnstile is not available within Mainland China."* The CN host is there for customers who are already inside that contract.

sections.title: Why you cannot fall back in the browser
sections.content:
The obvious mitigation — load the CN host, and if the challenge fails, retry against the global one — does not work. Reading the bundle shows why.

It recognises all three hosts and validates challenge origins against an allowlist:

```js
Wa = "https://challenges.cloudflare.com"
Ua = [Wa, "https://challenges.fed.cloudflare.com",
      "https://challenges.cloudflare-cn.com",
      "https://challenges-staging.cloudflare.com"]
```

There is even a `base-url` widget parameter that looks like it would let you override the challenge origin:

```js
function ir(params, allowBaseUrl, script) {
  var origin = script?.origin ?? Wa
  if (allowBaseUrl) return params["base-url"] ?? origin
  return origin
}
```

It is dead in production. Every call site passes `allowBaseUrl` as a literal `false`:

```js
Br(A, sitekey, params, rcV, /* allowBaseUrl */ !1, "b", ...)
```

And the origin itself is captured **once**, at script-eval time, from the `<script>` tag that loaded the bundle (`V = ya(); g.scriptUrlParsed = ...`). So `window.turnstile` is permanently bound to whichever host loaded it. You cannot re-point it, and loading a second copy from the other host does not re-bind it either.

Whichever host you choose is final for the life of the page. The decision has to be correct *before* the browser commits to it — which means it belongs on the server.

sections.title: Integrating it into an actual product
sections.content:
Around that time some users of [Prism](https://prism.siiway.org) could not complete the Turnstile login captcha at all. Locally hosted proof-of-work was tried as a workaround and was not a good fit. I applied this finding in [PR #14](https://github.com/siiway/prism/pull/14/changes/4b6f62aa9e8798bc553740e0e82a46f2fa00628d), switching users in China to the CN endpoint.

That shipped broken, for exactly the reason above: it kept using the site's single `region: "world"` sitekey and only swapped the host, so every visitor routed to China got `400020` and a login form that could never be submitted. Development used a test key, which passed.

The correct shape follows from the region field: the endpoint is a property of the **sitekey**, not of the visitor, so supporting both audiences means two widgets — two sitekey/secret pairs — chosen together with the host. The follow-up in Prism does that:

- A second, optional China widget alongside the global one.
- Host and sitekey are always chosen as a pair; the token comes back tagged with which widget minted it, so the server verifies against the matching secret.
- With no China widget configured, every China-leaning mode collapses to the global host. Choosing a mode you cannot support costs nothing.
- A configured China key is trusted only after the CN host confirms it will issue a challenge for it — cached, and run in the background so it never blocks a login page. That catches a key pasted into the wrong field, a widget that was actually created `region: "world"`, and a lapsed entitlement.

The general lesson is smaller than the mechanism: when a vendor gives you test credentials that take a different code path from real ones, a green light in development is not evidence.

sections.title: Quick how to use
sections.content:
**If you do not have China Network:** you cannot use this. A `region: "world"` sitekey is rejected by the CN host, your existing key cannot be converted, and the API will not let you create a China one. Stay on `https://challenges.cloudflare.com/turnstile/v0/api.js`.

**If you do:** create a second widget with `region: "china"` and switch the host *and* the sitekey together, per visitor.

| | Global | China |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Script | `challenges.cloudflare.com/turnstile/v0/api.js` | `challenges.cloudflare-cn.com/turnstile/v0/api.js` |
| Widget | `region: "world"` | `region: "china"` |
| Secret | that widget's secret | that widget's secret |

Server-side `siteverify` stays on the global host for both — only the secret changes, so keep track of which widget issued the token you are validating.

Route on something you can act on before render: request geolocation server-side, or browser language/timezone client-side. And gate the whole thing on the China key being present and working, so a misconfiguration degrades to the global host instead of locking people out.
